question: When solutions of lead(II) nitrate and potassium iodide are mixed, the reaction leads to the formation of which of the following?

options.text: A yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed.
A yellow precipitate of lead sulphate is formed.
An orange precipitate of lead iodide is formed.
An orange precipitate of lead iodate is formed.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When solutions of **lead(II) nitrate (Pb(NO₃)₂)** and **potassium iodide (KI)** are mixed, a double displacement reaction occurs.
 
• The reaction produces a yellow precipitate of **lead(II) iodide (PbI₂)**, which is insoluble in water. This is a characteristic property of lead iodide.
 
• The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is:

 **Pb(NO₃)₂ (aq) + 2KI (aq) → PbI₂ (s) + 2KNO₃ (aq)**
 
• The yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed due to the low solubility of PbI₂ in aqueous solution, which makes it settle as a solid.
 
• The potassium nitrate (KNO₃) formed remains dissolved in the solution as it is highly soluble in water.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lead(II) Nitrate [Pb(NO₃)₂]:**

 
 
• It is a white crystalline compound that is highly soluble in water.
 
• Lead(II) nitrate is commonly used in laboratories for reactions involving precipitation and in the preparation of other lead compounds.
 
 
 
• **Potassium Iodide (KI):**
 
 
• It is a white salt that dissolves readily in water to produce iodide ions (I⁻).
 
• Potassium iodide is often used in iodometry, as a dietary supplement, and in chemical reactions for iodide ion generation.
 
 
 
• **Lead(II) Iodide (PbI₂):**
 
 
• Lead iodide is a bright yellow solid that is sparingly soluble in cold water but more soluble in hot water.
 
• Upon heating, PbI₂ can dissolve and recrystallize when cooled, forming shiny golden plate-like crystals, often referred to as "golden rain."
 
 
 
• **Double Displacement Reaction:**
 
 
• This reaction involves the exchange of ions between two compounds to form new compounds.
 
• The reaction between Pb(NO₃)₂ and KI is a classic example of a double displacement reaction, resulting in the formation of an insoluble precipitate.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Solubility Rules:**

 
 
• Most nitrates (NO₃⁻) are soluble in water, which is why Pb(NO₃)₂ dissolves readily.
 
• Most iodides (I⁻) are soluble, except for those of lead (Pb²⁺), silver (Ag⁺), and mercury (Hg²⁺), making PbI₂ insoluble.
 
 
 
• **Practical Applications:**
 
 
• The formation of lead iodide is often used in school and college chemistry labs to demonstrate precipitation reactions.
 
• PbI₂ has applications in materials science, particularly in the fabrication of semiconductors and X-ray detectors.
